title: Cross-Cultural Calibration
hook: Every baseline you have was built in one culture; carry it into another and your calibration becomes a confident list of misreadings.
why:
By now your ledger has taught you roughly what your confidence is worth. That figure was earned somewhere particular: among people who talk at a certain volume, stand at a certain distance, hold eye contact for a certain time and fall silent for certain reasons. Move to another country, another region, another class, or simply another company with a different culture, and the figure is no longer true. Worse, it fails in a particular way. Your errors stop being scattered and start leaning in one direction, because you are measuring everyone against the same wrong ruler.

This chapter is about recalibrating when the ruler changes. It is not a catalogue of countries; Part V offers a working map, and any map is a starting point at best. It is a method: knowing where your own baselines came from, what the research does and does not say about how expression varies, how to build a local baseline from scratch, how to use people who know a setting better than you do, and how to avoid swapping one stereotype for another.

teach.p:
Every baseline you hold was built somewhere. Your sense of a normal speaking volume came from your family's kitchen. Your sense of how long a silence can last before it becomes uncomfortable came from the conversations you grew up in. Your sense of how much eye contact is honest and how much is rude came from your region, your class, your schools and your workplaces. None of it felt like culture while you were learning it. It felt like how people are.

This matters because the errors you make with an unfamiliar baseline are not random. A man raised among loud talkers will read a quiet room as cold, again and again, and each reading will feel like perception. A man raised where people touch freely will read a colleague's reserve as dislike. His ledger, if he keeps one, will show a run of confident misses all leaning the same way.

The research on emotion recognition shows the same shape at the level of whole groups. In 2002 Hillary Anger Elfenbein and Nalini Ambady combined nearly a hundred studies of people judging emotions in faces, voices and bodies across cultures. People recognised emotions at better than chance across cultural lines, so expression is far from arbitrary. But they were reliably more accurate with people from their own cultural group, and the advantage shrank where groups had more contact with each other. Familiarity is part of accuracy.

So the first step in any new setting is to remember that you have brought a ruler with you, and that it was made somewhere else. You cannot leave it at home. You can stop trusting it by default.

Before you read anyone abroad, ask what your home baseline would make of them, and then suspect that answer.
teach.disconfirm: If your ledger shows the same calibration in a new setting as at home, from the first week, your home baseline happens to fit this setting well. Check it separately for each kind of prediction before relaxing, because one kind can fit while another fails.
teach.pullQuote: You have brought a ruler with you, and it was made somewhere else.

teach.p:
Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen used the term display rules for the learned norms about who may show which feelings, to whom and how strongly. In a classic though small study reported in the early 1970s, Japanese and American students watched an unpleasant film. Alone, their faces reacted in similar ways. When an experimenter sat with them, the Japanese students more often masked their negative expressions with a smile. The feeling may have been the same. The display was governed by a rule about showing it in front of someone of higher status.

Later work has mapped display rules on a larger scale. In 2008 David Matsumoto and colleagues surveyed students in thirty-two countries about how much emotion they thought it right to show, and found that people in more individualistic countries endorsed more expression overall. Jeanne Tsai's research on what she calls ideal affect adds another layer: people in many East Asian settings tend to value calm, low-arousal good feelings, while many Americans value excitement. In a 2016 study, American leaders in official photographs showed broader, more excited smiles than Chinese leaders, who more often showed calm ones.

For a reader, the consequence is direct. A calm face may be contentment rather than indifference. A broad smile may be politeness rather than delight, or delight rather than politeness. A face that shows little in front of a senior person may show a great deal in front of a friend. The same muscles are being governed by different rules.

Display rules are also not only national. Workplaces, families, professions and generations have their own. A surgeon's face in theatre and a salesman's face on the floor follow different norms from the same man's face at home.

Learn the rules of a setting before you read the faces in it.
teach.disconfirm: If people in a new setting turn out to show the same feelings in the same ways and to the same degree as at home, in front of seniors and peers alike, the display rules there differ little from yours. Watch both kinds of audience before concluding it.

teach.p:
In 2010 Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan pointed out that most of what psychology knows about human beings comes from people who are Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic, which they abbreviated as WEIRD, and often from undergraduates in the United States. On a range of measures, from visual illusions to fairness, those people turned out to be unusual rather than typical. Many of the studies cited in this book share that limitation, and you should hold their findings as findings about the people studied.

Gaze is a good example of why it matters. Much Western advice treats steady eye contact as a sign of honesty and confidence. In 2013 a Japanese and Finnish team led by Hironori Akechi showed faces with direct and averted gaze to participants in Japan and Finland. Japanese participants rated faces making eye contact as angrier, less approachable and more unpleasant than Finnish participants did. A reader who brings the Western rule to such a setting will read respect as evasiveness and will himself come across as confrontational.

Context is treated differently too. In 2008 Takahiko Masuda and colleagues showed Japanese and American participants cartoons of a central figure surrounded by others. Japanese participants' judgments of the central figure's emotion were more influenced by the faces around it. The same face, read in two places, was read with different amounts of the room included.

None of this means that people in one culture cannot read people in another. It means that the rules you were taught as universal were very often local rules, and that the reader who checks which is which makes fewer confident mistakes.

When a rule in this book seems obvious, ask who it was tested on.
teach.disconfirm: If you find, in a new setting, that the gaze and context rules of your home culture predict people's reactions as well there as at home, the WEIRD caution does not bite in that setting. Test it with a ledger of a few dozen predictions before relying on it.

teach.p:
Some gestures are less like signals and more like words. Ekman and Friesen called them emblems: movements with a direct verbal translation that members of a group all know, such as a thumbs-up, a wave goodbye or a finger across the throat. Like words, they belong to languages, and the languages differ.

In 1979 Desmond Morris and his colleagues published the results of a survey across forty locations in Europe and around the Mediterranean, asking local people what twenty common gestures meant. The answers varied enormously. A thumb and forefinger joined in a ring meant *good* in some places, *zero* or *worthless* in others, and an obscene insult in others still. A backward toss of the head meant *no* in parts of Greece and southern Italy, and something else or nothing at all further north. Some of the boundaries ran through the middle of single countries.

The lesson is not to memorise a list. Lists go out of date, vary within countries, and tempt you to read emblems where there are none. The lesson is that any gesture you make without thinking is a word in your language, and you should not assume it means the same thing elsewhere. Notice which gestures you use most, and in a new setting, use fewer of them until you have seen how they land.

Head nods deserve special care, because they carry the conversation along without anyone noticing, and the patterns of nodding for yes, no, and *I'm listening* differ between places. The chapter on the head nod in Part III takes them up in detail.

When you do not know what a gesture means, the person who made it can tell you.
teach.disconfirm: If the gestures you use without thinking turn out to be understood as you intend in a new setting, by people of different ages and backgrounds there, your vocabulary happens to be shared. Ask a local informant to confirm before relying on it.

teach.h: The variation inside a culture is wider than the gap between cultures.
teach.p:
Once you learn that a culture tends towards reserve or towards expressiveness, it is very tempting to read every member of it that way. That is simply a new stereotype replacing the old baseline, and it fails just as badly.

Researchers who compare countries are usually careful to say that their findings describe averages. In most cross-cultural studies of expression and display rules, the spread of individuals within each country is wide, and the distributions of different countries overlap heavily. A quiet American and a voluble Finn are both easy to find. Region, class, generation, profession, personality and the setting of the moment all shape how a person shows what they feel, and a national average says little about the person in front of you.

This is why the method of this book, which starts from an individual baseline, matters more across cultures, not less. A cultural norm can tell you what range of behaviour to expect in a setting, so that you do not read ordinary reserve as hostility. It cannot tell you where this person sits within that range. Only watching this person over time can do that.

The practical rule has two parts. Use the cultural norm to widen your idea of what normal looks like, so that unfamiliar behaviour is not automatically read as a signal. Then use the individual baseline, as always, to look for change. A colleague who is quiet in a quiet office is at baseline. A colleague who is usually lively and goes quiet in that same office has changed, and the culture does not explain it.

Culture sets the range. The person sets the baseline.
teach.disconfirm: If, in a setting you know well, people turn out to behave very uniformly, so that knowing their culture tells you nearly everything about each person, the variation in that setting is unusually small. Check by comparing a dozen people's baselines on the same dimension.
teach.pullQuote: Culture sets the range. The person sets the baseline.

teach.h: Build a local baseline from scratch.
teach.p:
When you arrive in a setting whose norms you do not know, treat yourself as a beginner again, deliberately. Lower your confidence by at least one band by default, and for the first two weeks or so make descriptions rather than predictions.

Start with the neutral moments, the ones in which nothing much is at stake: greetings, small talk, queues, the start of meetings. Watch for a short list of dimensions. How loudly do people talk, and how fast? How close do they stand, and do they touch? How long do they hold eye contact, and with whom? How long are the silences before someone speaks? How much do faces move, and do smiles come easily? How do people interrupt, and how do they disagree?

Compare people with each other, not with home. The question is not whether this colleague is louder than your friends at home. It is whether he is louder than his colleagues here. Write these observations in your journal under a heading of their own, *local baseline*, so that you can see the setting's range building up.

When you begin to make predictions again, start with wide bands and harmless public behaviour, as in the calibration chapter: who will speak first, whether a greeting will include a handshake, how long a silence will last. Score them separately from your home ledger. Your calibration in the new setting is a new curve, and it starts flat.

Expect to feel clumsy. Being clumsy for a while is how you avoid being confidently wrong for a long time.
teach.disconfirm: If after a month your local predictions are as well calibrated as your home ones from the first day you resumed predicting, you may have needed less of a reset than this block assumes. Keep the separate ledger anyway until the curves agree for several months.

teach.p:
Anthropologists have always relied on informants, people inside a community who can explain what an outsider is seeing. For a reader of people in an unfamiliar setting, a good informant is worth more than any book, including this one.

The best informants know both your setting and theirs: a colleague who has worked in your country, a friend who grew up between two cultures. Ask them about behaviour, not about peoples. *When Mikko went quiet after the reallocation was announced, what would that usually mean here?* is a useful question. *Are Finns always this quiet?* invites a stereotype in return. Ask about variation too: *Would that be the same for someone older, or from the north?*

Use more than one informant where you can, because each one sees their culture from their own position within it, with their own class, generation and agenda. Where two informants disagree, you have learned that the behaviour varies, which is itself useful. Be wary of informants who seem to enjoy explaining their own people as a type.

In 1998 Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-García, writing about the training of doctors, argued for what they called cultural humility rather than cultural competence. Competence suggests a skill that can be completed. Humility is a lasting habit of self-questioning: you expect to be wrong, you ask, and you treat the other person as the authority on their own life. That is the right stance for a reader too.

And offer the same help in return. Being a good informant about your own culture is the simplest way to show that you are asking out of respect.
teach.disconfirm: If an informant's explanations of behaviour in their setting repeatedly fail to predict what happens next, either the informant is describing an ideal rather than practice, or their position within the culture differs from the people you are reading. Find a second informant before trusting either.

poseGallery.doCaption: Noticing that here, a lowered gaze to a senior is respect.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding the steady eye contact that reads as honest at home.
poseGallery.annotation: Gaze rules are among the most local of all. The same eye contact can be warmth in one place and challenge in another.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting the other person set the distance, and staying there.
poseGallery.annotation: Comfortable distance is learned. In a new setting, let others place themselves and follow their lead.

poseGallery.doCaption: Watching how people greet and gesture before doing it yourself.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Using a home gesture without checking what it means here.
poseGallery.annotation: Emblems are local vocabulary. Use fewer of yours until you have seen how they land.

poseGallery.doCaption: Reading him against his colleagues here: ordinary.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading a quiet colleague by your home baseline: cold.
poseGallery.annotation: Culture sets the range of normal. Compare people with each other in the setting, then look for change in the person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Returning the greeting you were given, at its depth
poseGallery.dontCaption: Performing the deepest version of a custom you have read about
poseGallery.annotation: Follow local customs as a guest, not as a performance. Let your host set the form.

caseStudy:
Daniel, thirty-nine, a project lead from Chicago, moves to his company's office in Helsinki for two years. In his first fortnight he reads the room as he would at home. Several colleagues leave long pauses before answering, show little on their faces when he presents, and rarely interrupt. He concludes that his ideas are not landing and that the team resents an outsider. His ledger, which he keeps separately for the new office, fills with confident predictions of objections that never come.

He lowers his confidence by a band and spends the next three weeks describing rather than predicting. He writes a local baseline: how long the silences usually last, who speaks first, how disagreement sounds when it comes. He finds that it comes directly and briefly, usually after the pause rather than as an interruption.

He also finds an informant. Aino, a colleague who spent six years in Toronto, tells him that in this office a long pause after a question usually means someone is thinking about it seriously. She adds that it varies: the younger engineers are quicker to jump in, and the sales team are different again.

Then Daniel overcorrects. He decides that silence here means nothing, and stops noticing it. A month later Mikko, who is usually the liveliest person in the room and the first to joke, sits through a whole meeting about the reallocation of projects without a word. Daniel's new rule says silence is normal. His individual baseline for Mikko says this is a large change.

He trusts the individual baseline and asks Mikko for a coffee. Mikko tells him that the reallocation takes him off the project he started, and that nobody asked him. Daniel arranges for him to stay on as an adviser. In his journal he writes a single line: *the office sets the range; Mikko sets the baseline.*
observe: The next time you are with people whose background differs from yours, notice one behaviour you were about to read through your own baseline, and what else it could mean in theirs.
In a setting new to you, notice how people greet each other, including distance, touch and eye contact, before you greet anyone yourself.
Notice one way your own family's baseline differs from a friend's family, for example in volume, touch or how an argument sounds.

drills.name: Map Your Own Baseline
steps: Write down your own default on eight dimensions: volume, speed, distance, touch, eye contact, length of silences, how easily you smile, and how you interrupt.
For each, note where you learned it: family, region, class, school or work.
Mark the ones you had assumed were simply how people are.
Ask someone from a different background to mark where their default differs from yours.
Write down the two differences most likely to cause you to misread someone.
variations: Repeat the drill for the setting you spend most time in now, such as your workplace, and compare it with your childhood defaults.
Ask two people from different backgrounds to mark your defaults, and compare where they each see you as unusual.
Write down one misreading from your journal that one of your defaults probably caused, and what it would have taken to avoid it.

drills.name: Local Baseline
steps: In a setting whose norms you do not know well, choose neutral moments such as greetings, queues or the start of meetings.
Make ten descriptive observations on the eight dimensions, with no predictions.
Compare the people you watch with each other, not with people at home.
Write the range you observed for each dimension under the heading local baseline.
Repeat on at least three days before you begin to make predictions in this setting.
variations: Build a local baseline for a setting within your own country that you rarely enter, such as a different kind of workplace or community event.
Ask an informant to read your local baseline notes and tell you which observations surprise them.
Repeat the baseline a month later and note which of your first observations held up and which changed.

drills.name: Informant Interview
steps: Choose someone who knows a setting well and, ideally, also knows yours.
Prepare three questions about specific behaviour you have seen, such as what a long pause after a question would usually mean here.
Ask each, and follow it with a question about variation, such as whether it would differ for someone older or from elsewhere.
Write down the answers as close to their words as you can.
Ask a second informant the same questions within a fortnight and note where the two differ.
variations: Ask your informant how you come across in their setting, and which of your habits might be misread.
Interview an informant about a setting you think you already know well, and note anything that surprises you.
Ask a question about variation by age or region for every behaviour you discuss, and record the answers separately.

drills.name: Separate Ledgers
steps: Take your scored predictions about people whose background differs from yours, at least twenty of them.
Draw their calibration curve separately from the rest of your ledger.
Compare the two curves band by band.
Where the cross-cultural curve shows overconfidence, drop your stated confidence by one band for that kind of prediction.
Write the adjustment and a date to check it again at the front of your ledger.
variations: Separate your cross-cultural predictions further, by setting, and see whether your overconfidence is the same in each.
Check whether your cross-cultural misses lean in one direction, such as reading people as colder or more hostile than they were.
Compare your cross-cultural curve after three months with your first one, and note which bands have moved.

drills.name: Gesture Check
steps: List five gestures you use without thinking, such as a thumbs-up, a beckoning finger, a ring of thumb and forefinger, pointing and nodding.
For each, find out from a reliable source or an informant where its meaning differs.
Mark any you should avoid or check in settings you expect to visit.
Choose a neutral alternative for each marked gesture, such as words or an open hand.
Practise the alternatives in front of a mirror until they feel natural.
variations: Ask an informant which of your everyday gestures they noticed when they first met you, and what they thought they meant.
Watch a recorded conversation from a setting you do not know with the sound off, and list the gestures you could not interpret.
Spend a day using words instead of your three most common gestures, and note whether anyone responds differently.

quiz.q: You have spent years building well-calibrated baselines at home. In a new country, how far should you trust your readings at first?
options: As far as at home, since the basic emotions are shown the same everywhere
Less than at home, since your errors will tend to lean in one direction
More than at home, since outsiders see things that locals have stopped noticing
Not at all, since people from other cultures cannot be read by outsiders
quiz.explain: Your baselines were built in one culture, so in another your errors stop being scattered and lean the same way. Lower your confidence by a band, describe before you predict, and build a local baseline.

quiz.q: What did Elfenbein and Ambady's 2002 meta-analysis find about recognising emotions across cultures?
options: It was above chance across cultures, and better within one's own group
It fell to chance level whenever the two cultures involved were different
It was equally accurate whatever the culture of the person making the judgment
It was only possible for observers who had been trained in other cultures
quiz.explain: Expression is far from arbitrary, since people recognised emotions across cultural lines. But familiarity helped: people were more accurate with their own group, and the advantage shrank with more contact between groups.

quiz.q: In Friesen's study of Japanese and American students watching an unpleasant film, what changed when an experimenter sat with them?
options: Both groups of students showed more disgust in front of the experimenter
The American students hid their reactions more completely than before
Neither group's expressions changed at all when someone else was present
The Japanese students more often masked negative feelings with a smile
quiz.explain: Alone, both groups reacted similarly. With a higher-status person present, a display rule came into play for the Japanese students. The feeling may have been the same, while the display was governed by a learned norm.

quiz.q: In an office abroad where meetings are often quiet, a colleague who is usually the liveliest in the room goes silent through a whole meeting. What fits?
options: Ignore it, since silence in meetings is normal in this office
Read it as disapproval, as you would read it in an office at home
Treat it as a change from his own baseline, and ask him privately
Ask a local colleague what people in this country mean by silence
quiz.explain: The office's norm sets the range of normal, but this man's own baseline is lively, so his silence is a change that the culture does not explain. Asking him privately tests the reading without assuming anything about his culture.

quiz.q: What was the main concern Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan raised about WEIRD samples?
options: That Western researchers had been deliberately excluding other countries
That results from Western samples are always wrong when tested elsewhere
That much of psychology rests on narrow samples whose results may not travel
That people outside the West are less willing to take part in research
quiz.explain: Most research participants have been Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic, and on many measures they turned out to be unusual. Findings about them are findings about them until they are tested elsewhere.

quiz.q: You will be working for a month in a country you have never visited. What is the best first step for your reading of people there?
options: Memorise a list of the country's gestures and their meanings before you go
Describe rather than predict at first, and build a local baseline
Read people exactly as you would at home and correct mistakes as they come
Avoid reading anyone until you have lived there for at least a year
quiz.explain: A list is a starting point that varies within countries and goes out of date. Watching neutral moments, comparing people with each other and finding an informant gives you a baseline for the setting you are actually in.

quiz.q: What did Akechi and colleagues find in 2013 when they showed faces with direct and averted gaze to participants in Japan and Finland?
options: Both groups rated faces making eye contact as warmer and more approachable than faces looking away
Japanese participants rated faces making eye contact as angrier and less approachable than Finns did
Finnish participants rated faces looking away as more honest than faces making direct eye contact
Neither group noticed any difference between the faces making eye contact and those looking away
quiz.explain: Japanese participants rated faces making eye contact as angrier, less approachable and more unpleasant than Finnish participants did. A reader who carries the Western rule that steady eye contact signals honesty can read respect as evasion, and come across as confrontational.

quiz.q: What did Masuda and colleagues find in 2008 when Japanese and American participants judged the emotion of a central figure in a cartoon?
options: American participants were more influenced than Japanese ones by the faces of the surrounding figures
Neither group took any notice of the faces around the central figure when they made their judgments
Both groups ignored the central figure and rated only the faces of the people standing around it
Japanese participants' judgments of the central figure were more influenced by the faces around it
quiz.explain: The same face, read in two places, was read with different amounts of the room included. Rules about how much context to use in reading a face are learned, like other display rules.

quiz.q: A colleague says the ring made with thumb and forefinger means OK everywhere. What did Morris and his colleagues find in their 1979 survey?
options: It meant good in some places, zero or worthless in others, and an obscene insult in others still
It meant OK everywhere they asked, which is why it is used as a universal sign in airports and hotels
It meant nothing at all in most of the forty locations, so people simply ignored it when they saw it
It was used only by divers and pilots, and almost no ordinary people anywhere recognised its meaning
quiz.explain: Gestures like this are emblems, local vocabulary rather than universal signals. Any gesture you make without thinking is a word in your own language, and you should not assume it means the same thing elsewhere.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific time when you misread someone whose background differed from yours, at work, while travelling, or in your own neighbourhood. What did you see, and what did you conclude using your own baseline? What would the behaviour more likely have meant in theirs, and how did you find out, if you did? What would you do in the first ten minutes of a similar meeting now?
reflection.guidance: The background does not have to be national. Many of the clearest examples come from class, region, generation or profession, which can differ as much as countries do. Try to name the dimension involved, such as volume, distance or silence, and the home baseline you were using without knowing it. Your answer to the last question should be something you can actually do.

failureMode: The first failure is to carry your home baselines everywhere and to read unfamiliar norms as signals, which produces a steady run of confident misreadings that all lean the same way. The second is the overcorrection: replacing the old baseline with a national stereotype, so that every member of a culture is read as its average, and the change in one person is missed. The third is catalogue thinking, trusting lists of gestures and customs over local observation and informants. The fourth is performance, copying local customs as a show rather than following them as a guest. The last is withdrawal: deciding that people unlike you cannot be read, and so not trying, which looks like humility and works like avoidance.

moreCases.title: The volunteer teacher and the lowered gaze
moreCases.scene:
Ruth, sixty-one, a retired secondary teacher, volunteers twice a week at an English class for adults who have recently arrived in the country. Most of her students are women, but one of the most regular is Yusuf, fifty-four, who was an accountant before he left his home country. He works hard and his written English is good.

When Ruth corrects his pronunciation in front of the class, Yusuf looks down at the table and stays looking down until she moves on. He never meets her eye during a correction. After a few weeks Ruth begins to read this as sullenness, perhaps resentment at being corrected by a woman, and she starts correcting him less, which she tells herself is tact.

Another volunteer, Kemal, who interprets for the class and grew up in the same region as Yusuf, notices the change and asks her about it. Ruth explains. Kemal tells her that where he and Yusuf grew up, many men of Yusuf's generation were taught to lower their eyes when an older person or a teacher corrects them, as a sign of respect, and that looking up would feel to Yusuf like answering back. He adds that it varies a good deal: his own children look teachers in the eye without a second thought, and so do several of the younger students in the class.

Ruth had taught for thirty years in a school where she regularly told pupils, *Look at me when I'm talking to you*, and had never thought of the instruction as local.
moreCases.misread:
Ruth read Yusuf's lowered gaze through her own classroom's ruler, where looking down during a correction meant sulking. She then built a story about resentment on top of it, and adjusted her teaching to the story, so that Yusuf received less of the help he had come for.

She also read her own decision to correct him less as sensitivity, when it was a quiet withdrawal of teaching based on a story she had never checked.
moreCases.betterRead:
This is the Akechi finding in a single classroom: eye contact and its absence carry different meanings in different settings, and a reader who brings the home rule will read respect as evasion. Kemal was a good informant in the way the chapter describes. He explained a behaviour, not a people, and he volunteered the variation within his own community. Ruth's next step was the individual baseline. She noticed that Yusuf looked at her readily in conversation before and after class, and laughed easily with the other students, which made sullenness an unlikely reading. She went back to correcting him as she did everyone else. A month later he asked her, in careful English, whether she could correct him more.

Ruth also asked Kemal whether there was anything about her own behaviour in class that the students might find hard to read.

Kemal's point about variation mattered as much as his explanation. Ruth had nearly swapped one rule for another, *looking down means respect*, and the younger students would have broken it the next week.

moreCases.title: The sales director with a printed guide
moreCases.scene:
Mark, fifty, is preparing for his first sales visit to a country he has never been to. The night before he flies, he reads an online guide to doing business there, and prints the page of body language tips. It says that people there rarely say no directly, that a smile can hide disagreement, that silence often means refusal, and that you should never show the soles of your feet.

At the first meeting his host, Mrs Okafor, a procurement director in her forties, listens to his proposal, asks three precise questions about delivery times, and then says, smiling, *No. That price does not work for us. If you can do better, call me next week.*

Mark, remembering the guide, reads the smile as the real message and the no as politeness. He keeps the meeting going for another forty minutes, presenting the same price in different ways, waiting for her to come round. She looks at her watch twice, then stands, shakes his hand warmly and thanks him for coming.

He flies home convinced that the meeting went well, and is surprised when she does not take his calls. A colleague who knows her says that Mrs Okafor is famous for her bluntness, which she learned during ten years working in Rotterdam.

In the taxi back to his hotel, he underlines the line in the guide about smiles, pleased that it had been so accurate.
moreCases.misread:
Mark read Mrs Okafor through a printed list instead of through her own behaviour. The guide told him that a smile hides a no; her words told him a smile came with one. He believed the list over the person, and read her clear refusal as an opening.

He also read her two glances at her watch, and her warm handshake as she ended the meeting, through the same list, as signs that she was keen to continue the conversation another time.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter's warning about catalogue thinking is exactly this. Lists go out of date, vary within countries, and tempt you to read hidden meanings where the person has been direct. Culture sets the range; the person sets the baseline. A national average said little about a procurement director with her own career and her own style, and her own words were the best evidence in the room. The cheapest test would have been to take her at her word and ask: *If I can come back with a better price, what would it need to be?* On his next visit Mark left the printout at home. He watched how she behaved in the first minutes, asked directly what she needed, and when she said no again, believed her.

He also wrote to Mrs Okafor, thanked her for her time and asked whether he could send a revised price. She replied the same day.

moreCases.title: The start-up recruit in the quiet firm
moreCases.scene:
Tom, twenty-eight, spent five years at a fast-growing software start-up where people showed enthusiasm loudly. Good ideas were greeted with whoops in the stand-up meeting, managers wrote *Love this!!* on proposals, and a flat response meant a dead idea. He has just joined a long-established engineering firm as a product manager.

In his first month he presents three proposals to his new manager, Gillian, fifty-six. Each time she listens, nods slowly, asks one or two questions, and says something like *That seems sensible. Let's see what the team think.* Her face barely moves. Tom reads each response as polite rejection. By the third, he has started to wonder whether he made a mistake in taking the job, and tells a friend that his manager does not rate him.

At his one-month review, Gillian tells him that his proposals have been the best thing to happen to the department in a year, that two of them are already being costed, and that she has mentioned him to the director. Tom is astonished. He asks her, carefully, why she did not say so at the time. She looks puzzled and says that she did.

In the same month, two of his old colleagues message him to ask how the new job is going, and he tells both of them that he is not sure it is working out.
moreCases.misread:
Tom read Gillian's calm, low-key responses through the display rules of his old workplace, where excitement was the currency of approval and calm meant indifference. In her setting, calm approval was approval.

He also read his own anxiety in the meetings as information about Gillian's view, when it came from the gap between two sets of rules.

And he read his friend's sympathy, when he complained, as confirmation, though the friend knew nothing about Gillian at all.
moreCases.betterRead:
Display rules are not only national. Workplaces, professions and generations have their own, and Jeanne Tsai's work on ideal affect gives a name to the difference Tom ran into: some settings value calm, low-arousal good feelings, and others value excitement. *That seems sensible* in Gillian's mouth was strong praise. Tom's fix was to build a local baseline for the new firm as he would for a new country. He watched how Gillian and others responded to ideas they plainly liked, such as a colleague's plan that was adopted the same week, and found that it sounded just like what she had said to him. He also stopped reading his own discomfort as information about her.

He also told Gillian, at the end of the review, how he had read her responses, which made her laugh and then change how she gave feedback to him.

moreCases.title: The manager who decided they could not be read
moreCases.scene:
Graham, fifty-five, manages an engineering team split between his own office and a partner office in another country, which he visits four times a year. On his first visit he misread a quiet meeting badly, assuming that the team opposed a plan they in fact supported, and was embarrassed when it came out. Since then he has decided that he simply cannot read people there, and that it would be presumptuous to try. On calls with the partner team he looks at his notes, listens to the words and leaves it at that. He tells himself this is cultural humility.

Wei, thirty-two, is one of the partner office's strongest engineers. For two years she has been one of the most talkative people on the calls: she jokes with the British team, asks questions and argues when she disagrees. Over the past six weeks she has said almost nothing. Her camera, which used to be on, has been off for the last four calls.

Graham does not notice. A colleague in his own office, Priya, does. She mentions to Graham that Wei seems to have gone quiet, and asks whether he knows why.

Graham had kept a careful ledger for his own office for a year. He had stopped keeping one for the partner office after the first visit.

On the most recent call, when the British team asked for volunteers to review a design, Wei's name was not among them, for the first time anyone could remember.
moreCases.misread:
Graham read his withdrawal from reading as humility. It worked as avoidance: by deciding that nobody in the partner office could be read, he stopped watching the one thing that works in any setting, the change in an individual against her own baseline.

He had also read his first misreading as proof that the partner office was unreadable, rather than as one miss in a setting where he had no baseline yet.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter names this failure: withdrawal looks like humility and works like avoidance. Cultural humility means expecting to be wrong and asking, not ceasing to notice. Graham did not need to know anything about the partner office's norms to see that Wei had changed. Her baseline, built over two years of calls, was talkative, questioning and on camera, and she had moved far from it. Priya's question was the prompt he needed. He asked Wei for a private call, said that she had seemed quieter lately and asked how things were going. Wei told him that her role had been restructured locally in a way that cut her out of design decisions, and that she was thinking of leaving.

Graham started keeping a ledger for the partner office again, beginning with descriptions rather than predictions.

Graham also told Priya that she had been right to ask, and that he had been calling avoidance humility for two years.

workedReading.title: Lunch with a louder family
workedReading.scene:
Sam, twenty-nine, grew up in a small, quiet family in a village, where meals were calm and voices were rarely raised. His partner, Becky, is one of six siblings in a large, loud family, and Sam has been invited to his first Sunday lunch with all of them, including Becky's grandfather, who is eighty-four. Sam has been working through this book and decides to treat the lunch as a new setting, using the chapter's method. He also decides that he will not take notes, read anyone aloud or treat the family as practice material. He will simply notice, and write a few lines in his journal afterwards.

Becky has warned him that her family can be a lot, and has promised to rescue him if he looks lost.

He knows his own family's quiet has its own rules, and that Becky found his parents' silences hard to read the first time she met them.

steps.label: Name the home ruler
steps.text:
On the drive there, Sam asks himself what his own family would make of a typical lunch at Becky's, from what she has told him. The answer is uncomfortable: raised voices would mean a row, interruptions would mean rudeness, and someone who said nothing would be in a sulk. He reminds himself that this is his ruler, made in his parents' kitchen, and that it is very likely to be wrong in this one. He resolves to lower his confidence in any reading by a band and to describe rather than conclude for the first hour.

He also reminds himself that he is the unfamiliar one, and that his own quietness will be read through their ruler.

steps.label: Describe, don't predict
steps.text:
For the first hour he simply notices. Everyone talks loudly and fast. People interrupt constantly, and nobody seems to mind. Two of Becky's brothers argue fiercely about football, almost shouting, and then one of them passes the other the potatoes with a grin. People touch a great deal: hands on shoulders, a hug at every arrival. Silences almost never last more than a second. Sam notices the urge, several times, to read tension, and lets it pass.

He notices, too, that his own silences are being filled within a second by someone else, which he finds restful rather than rude.

He writes none of this down at the table. He simply lets each observation sit, as a description, without a verdict attached.

steps.label: Compare them with each other
steps.text:
Instead of comparing the family with his own, he compares them with each other. The football argument is louder than anything at his parents' table, but no louder than the argument Becky's aunt and mother have about a holiday, which ends in laughter. The volume is the range here, not a signal. Becky's youngest sister is quieter than the rest, but she interrupts as freely as anyone when she has something to say. Becky's father is the loudest of all. Within this family, loud is ordinary.

He also notices that nobody looks offended when interrupted, and that interruptions here seem to show interest rather than disrespect.

steps.label: Find the grandfather's baseline
steps.text:
The one person who worries Sam is Becky's grandfather, who has hardly said a word at the table and has not looked at Sam once. Sam's home ruler offers disapproval. But Sam remembers that an hour earlier, in the garden, the grandfather had talked to him for ten minutes about his tomatoes, cheerfully and at length. That is a baseline, and the table is a change from it. Sam looks for a rival. At the table, the noise is overwhelming, and he notices that the grandfather wears hearing aids.

He also notices that the grandfather's hearing aids whistle once when the noise is loudest, which makes the rival reading stronger.

steps.label: Ask the informant
steps.text:
After the main course, washing up with Becky, Sam asks her quietly whether her grandfather is always this quiet at lunch. Becky says that he is, now, and that it started a couple of years ago, when his hearing got worse. He finds the noise impossible, she says, and gives up trying to follow. She adds that her grandfather had asked her earlier whether Sam was the one who knew about gardening, and had seemed pleased. Sam realises that the reading his ruler offered, disapproval, would have been exactly wrong.

He thanks Becky and does not mention that he had nearly read her grandfather as hostile. That reading was his, and it can stay in the journal.

steps.label: Test it gently
steps.text:
Over pudding, Sam moves to the chair next to the grandfather, at the quieter end of the table, and asks him, clearly and facing him, how he gets his tomatoes to ripen so early. The grandfather turns to him at once and talks for a quarter of an hour, smiling, with his hand on Sam's arm for part of it. Becky's mother catches Becky's eye across the table and raises her eyebrows. Sam is not sure what that means, and decides not to guess.

He also notices that the noise at the table drops slightly while the two of them talk, as if the family were listening.

steps.label: What went in the journal
steps.text:
That night Sam writes a few lines. *Local baseline at Becky's: loud, fast, constant interrupting, lots of touch. Arguments end in laughter. Silence is rare and means little at the table. Grandfather: talkative one to one, silent in the noise, probably hearing. My ruler said row, rudeness and disapproval. All three wrong.* He adds one more line: *Ask Becky what her mum's eyebrows meant.* Becky tells him, a week later, that it meant her mother approved.

The journal entry is about the family's norms and his own ruler, not about any of them as individuals, and he does not show it to anyone.

moreFailures.title: Using culture to explain away a change
moreFailures.body:
Once you know something about a setting's norms, it becomes tempting to file every surprise under culture. A colleague in an overseas office goes quiet, and you think: they are often quiet there. A neighbour from a different background seems withdrawn, and you think: perhaps that is normal for them. Sometimes it is. But culture explains the range, not the change. A person who has been lively for two years and goes quiet has moved against their own baseline, and the culture they share with their colleagues did not change at the same moment. Using culture to explain a change is a quiet way of not asking, and it falls hardest on the people you are least familiar with, whose distress then goes unnoticed for longest. When an individual changes, treat it as you would anywhere: as a change, worth a gentle question.

A useful check: if you would ask a colleague from home about the same change, ask this one too.

It also protects you from a subtler error: treating a person's ordinary behaviour as cultural when it is simply who they are, which is a way of seeing their background before you see them.

moreFailures.title: Asking one person to speak for a whole people
moreFailures.body:
A colleague from another country, or a friend with a background you do not share, can be a valuable informant. They can also become an unwilling one. Being asked again and again to explain *your people*, to say what everyone from somewhere thinks or does, is tiring, and it puts the person in an impossible position, since nobody can speak for millions of others. It also invites the stereotype the chapter warns against, because the easiest answer to a question about a people is a generalisation. Ask about specific behaviour you have seen, ask about variation, and ask only people who have offered to help or whose role it is. Use more than one informant, and offer the same help about your own background in return. Thank them, and do not make them the office's permanent explainer.

Remember, too, that informants are people with their own positions and agendas. An informant's account of their culture is evidence, not the final word.

moreFailures.title: Forgetting that you are the unfamiliar one
moreFailures.body:
In a new setting you are reading people through a ruler made elsewhere, and they are reading you through theirs. Your volume, your eye contact, your distance and your gestures all carry meanings you did not intend. A reader who concentrates on decoding others can forget that he is producing signals that are being decoded too, often less charitably than he decodes them. A man used to steady eye contact may come across as confrontational; one used to standing close may seem pushy; one used to animated gestures may seem agitated. Part of a local baseline is noticing how people respond to you: who steps back, who looks away, who goes quiet when you raise your voice. Adjust modestly, as a guest would, and ask an informant how you come across.

You will often find that people in the new setting are making the same allowances for you that you are learning to make for them.

You might also ask a colleague at home how you seem when you return from abroad. Changes you have made without noticing can tell you which local norms you have absorbed.

moreFailures.title: Reading the timing in an interpreted conversation
moreFailures.body:
When a conversation runs through an interpreter, its timing is scrambled. The other person reacts to your words only after the interpreter has spoken them, so their face responds several seconds late and to the interpreter's phrasing rather than yours. Long pauses are built into the rhythm. A reader who applies the usual rules about the timing of a change will see hesitation where there is only translation, and will read a delayed smile as forced. Watch the other person's reactions against the interpreter's words, not your own, and treat pauses as part of the process. Look at the interpreter too: their own reactions can tell you whether a phrase has landed awkwardly. Most of all, ask more explicit questions than you normally would, because the channels you usually rely on are partly blocked.

If you can, meet the interpreter beforehand and ask them about anything you should know about the other person's style.

Remember that the interpreter is choosing words for you. A reaction to a phrase you did not use is information about the translation, not about the person.

questions.q: Isn't it a form of stereotyping to learn about cultural norms at all?
questions.a:
It becomes stereotyping when you apply an average to an individual. Learning that a setting tends towards longer silences or more reserved faces is useful if you use it to widen your idea of what normal looks like, so that you do not read ordinary behaviour there as a signal. It becomes harmful when you use it to predict how a particular person will behave, or to explain away what they do. The chapter's rule is the safeguard: culture sets the range, the person sets the baseline. Hold cultural knowledge as a set of possibilities, check it against the person in front of you and against informants, and drop it the moment the person's own behaviour tells you something different.

If you notice yourself saying *they* about a whole people, stop and ask whether you mean the setting or a person.

A good test is whether you would be comfortable having your cultural knowledge read aloud to the person it is about. If it sounds like a description of a range, it probably helps; if it sounds like a verdict, it does not.

questions.q: How can I tell whether a difference I notice is cultural or personal?
questions.a:
Compare the person with others in the same setting, not with people at home. If most people in a meeting leave long pauses before answering, a long pause from one of them is probably the setting's norm. If one person behaves very differently from everyone around them, the difference is more likely to be personal. Time helps too: a behaviour that is consistent across weeks and situations is part of the person's baseline, whatever its source. Informants can tell you whether something is common where they come from, and two informants who disagree tell you that it varies. In practice the distinction matters less than it seems, because either way the useful question is what is normal for this person, and whether it has changed.

Personality varies within every culture, so a quiet person in a talkative setting is not necessarily reserved by upbringing; they may simply be quiet.

questions.q: What if I am the one from a minority background, and people at work keep misreading me?
questions.a:
It is not your job to fix other people's calibration, and it is tiring to be misread. But some things can help. You can name your own norms where it is useful, briefly and without apology: *When I go quiet in meetings, it usually means I'm thinking it through.* An ally who knows you well can say the same on your behalf. You can also ask directly when you suspect a misreading has happened, as you would with anyone. And notice that you probably already hold two rulers, one from home and one from work, which is an advantage in reading people that most of your colleagues do not have. If misreadings start to affect how you are treated or assessed, raise it with your manager or HR, as a matter of fairness rather than of manners.

You might also find it useful to keep your own journal of misreadings by others, as data rather than grievance. Patterns in it can help you decide when to name your norms and when to let something pass.

Most of all, do not let other people's misreadings persuade you that your own behaviour is wrong. Different rules are not worse ones.

questions.q: Should I copy local customs, such as greetings, when I visit somewhere new?
questions.a:
Follow them as a guest, modestly, after you have watched how they are done. Let your hosts lead: return the greeting you are given, at the depth and in the form you are given it, rather than performing the most elaborate version you have read about. Many hosts will greet a visitor in the visitor's own way to make them comfortable, and it is gracious to accept that. If you are unsure, ask someone. Getting a custom slightly wrong with good intentions is rarely a problem; performing it as a show, or copying it to seem like an insider, usually is. The chapter's failure list includes performance for this reason: following a custom is respect, but putting it on display makes it about you.

When you get it wrong, a smile and a simple apology are usually all that is needed.

It is also worth asking what your hosts would expect from you, which may be your own customs rather than theirs.

questions.q: How long does it take to build a reliable baseline in a new setting?
questions.a:
Longer than most people expect. The chapter suggests about two weeks of description before you start making predictions, and even then your calibration in the new setting is a new curve that starts flat. Expect it to take several months of scored predictions before your confidence there is worth as much as it is at home, and keep those predictions in a separate ledger so that you can see the curve develop. Individual baselines take time too: you need to see a person across several situations before you know what is normal for them. Some settings never feel as readable as home, and that is fine. Lower confidence, more questions and more help from informants are a sound way to work for as long as you need them.

Keep in mind that you are calibrating to a setting, not a country. Each new workplace or community has its own range, even within one place.

questions.q: Does any of this apply to people from my own country?
questions.a:
Very much so. Region, class, generation, profession, faith, workplace and family all have their own display rules and baselines, and the differences between them can be as large as those between countries. A manager from one part of a country can misread a team from another for years, and a person who moves from a start-up to a long-established firm meets a new set of rules about how to show approval. Families have their own norms too, as anyone who has spent Christmas with a partner's family knows. The method is the same everywhere: notice that you have brought a ruler, describe before you conclude, compare people with each other rather than with home, and ask someone who knows.

The advantage is that informants are much easier to find at home, and much more likely to share your language for describing what you are seeing.

The advantage of practising at home is that misreadings are easier to discover and cheaper to correct.

watch.title: Mr. Baseball: Official Trailer
watch.notice: An American baseball player struggles in Japan. Notice the collisions over bowing, directness and deference to the manager, and how slowly he learns to read the room.

reviewPrompt: In the next unfamiliar setting you enter, describe the local baseline on three dimensions before you make a single prediction about anyone there.
